steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported, making them available for use in the component.
successCriteria: The code should have a valid import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing local state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import statement. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package using an import statement.

steps.title: Import zustand from 'zustand'
steps.instruction: Import the create function from the 'zustand' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with the named export 'create' from the 'zustand' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing a function from a package
import { create } from 'zustand';
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Import create from 'zustand' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'zustand' package is imported, making the create function available for creating stores.
successCriteria: The import statement should import the named export 'create' from the 'zustand' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the create function from zustand, which is essential for creating global state stores.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing the 'create' function specifically from the 'zustand' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're importing the correct function from the correct package. You need to import 'create' from 'zustand'.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Define a functional component named App with proper TypeScript typing. The component should return a JSX element.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function. Make sure to specify the return type as JSX.Element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named App is created with TypeScript typing and returns JSX.
successCriteria: The component should be named App, have proper TypeScript typing (return type JSX.Element), and return a JSX element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the component is named App, has proper TypeScript typing, and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component is missing or incomplete. Ensure you define a functional component named App with TypeScript typing that returns JSX.

steps.title: Define the store interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named StoreState with two properties: count (number) and user (string).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with types.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a TypeScript interface that defines the shape of your global store state.
successCriteria: The code includes an interface named StoreState with count: number and user: string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the StoreState interface with the correct properties and types. This interface will ensure type safety when using your Zustand store.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface has both required properties with the correct TypeScript types: count should be number and user should be string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The StoreState interface is missing or incorrect. Make sure to define an interface named StoreState with count: number and user: string properties.

steps.title: Create the zustand store
steps.instruction: Create a zustand store using the 'create' function imported earlier. Use TypeScript generics with the StoreState interface to define the store's shape. Initialize the store with a count of 0 and an empty string for text.
steps.hint: Call create<StoreState>() with a function that returns an object containing the initial state values for count and text.
steps.expectedOutcome: A zustand store is created with proper TypeScript typing and initial state values.
successCriteria: The store should be created using create<StoreState> with an initial state object containing count: 0 and text: ''.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a zustand store with TypeScript generics and proper initial state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're using the StoreState interface with create<StoreState> and providing both count and text in the initial state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The store creation is incomplete. Make sure to use create<StoreState>() with a function that returns an object containing both count and text properties.

steps.title: Add increment action to the store
steps.instruction: Inside your store definition, add an increment action that increases the count property by 1.
steps.hint: Add a method to the set parameter that updates the state. Use the set function to modify the count property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The store now has an increment action that can be called to update the global count state.
successCriteria: The store definition includes an increment method that uses set to increase count by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the increment action to your Zustand store. This action will allow components to update the global count state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the increment action needs to properly update the count. Make sure it uses the set function to increase the count property by 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The store doesn't yet have a working increment action. Remember to add a method called 'increment' that uses set to update the count state.

steps.title: Add updateUser action to the store
steps.instruction: Add a user property to the StoreState interface and an updateUser action to the store that updates the user's name.
steps.hint: Extend the StoreState interface with a user object containing a name property, then add an updateUser action to the store that uses set to update the user.
steps.expectedOutcome: The StoreState interface should include a user property with a name field, and the store should have an updateUser action that updates the user's name.
successCriteria: The code should have a user property in StoreState and an updateUser action in the store that uses set to update the user.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a user property to the StoreState interface and an updateUser action to the store. This demonstrates how to handle nested state updates in Zustand.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added both the user property to the StoreState interface and the updateUser action to the store. The updateUser action should use set to update the user's name.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires adding a user property to the StoreState interface and an updateUser action to the store. Check the analogous example for the correct structure.

steps.title: Initialize local state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, create a local state variable called 'localName' using useState. Initialize it with an empty string.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the type as string.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a local state variable with useState
const [localName, setLocalName] = useState<string>('');
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a local state variable 'localName' initialized to an empty string, ready to be used alongside the global Zustand store.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call inside the App component that declares a variable named 'localName' with an initial value of an empty string and proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a local state variable using useState. This shows how component-specific state can coexist with global Zustand state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) Placed the useState call inside the App component, 2) Named the variable 'localName', 3) Initialized it with an empty string, and 4) Used proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Remember to use the useState hook inside the App component to create a state variable called 'localName' with an initial value of an empty string and string type annotation.

steps.title: Create the component structure
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, return a div container with the className 'app-container'.
steps.hint: Add a div element with the specified className inside the return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component returns a div with className 'app-container' containing the existing h1 element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the basic container structure for your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have a div with className 'app-container' that wraps the existing h1 element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're returning a div with className 'app-container' containing the h1 element.

steps.title: Display global count state
steps.instruction: Inside your component's JSX, display the current value of the global count state from the zustand store.
steps.hint: Use the useStore hook to access the count value, then render it inside your JSX.
steps.expectedOutcome: The global count value (0 initially) should be displayed in the component's output.
successCriteria: The component should use the useStore hook to access the count value and render it in JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully accessed and displayed the global count state from the zustand store.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're both accessing the count from the store and rendering it in your JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count value isn't being displayed. Remember to use the useStore hook to get the count and render it in your component.

steps.title: Add increment button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a button element with the text 'Increment' that calls the increment action from your Zustand store when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the useStore hook to access the increment action, then add a button with onClick={increment}.
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Increment' appears in the UI that, when clicked, will trigger the increment action from your Zustand store.
successCriteria: onClick handler that calls increment action
Proper destructuring of increment from useStore
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully added a button that calls the increment action when clicked. This connects your UI to the global state management provided by Zustand.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are a few issues. Make sure you're properly accessing the increment action from the useStore hook and wiring it to the button's onClick handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly connected to the increment action. Remember to use the useStore hook to access the increment function and pass it to the button's onClick prop.

steps.title: Add user update section with input and button
steps.instruction: Add an input field and button to update the user name in the store. The input should be controlled by the localName state, and the button should call the updateUser action from the store.
steps.hint: Add an input element with value={localName} and onChange handler to update localName. Add a button with onClick that calls updateUser with the current localName value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The app will have a text input and a button that allows updating the user name in the global store.
successCriteria: Add an input element with type="text"
The input has onChange handler that updates localName
Add a button with onClick that calls updateUser(localName)
The button has text content like 'Update User'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the user update section with a controlled input and button that updates the global store.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both the input and button with the correct attributes and handlers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The user update section is missing or incomplete. Check that you have an input with value and onChange, and a button with onClick that calls updateUser.
